# Shared-Identifier Clustering

When records that are *supposed* to be independent share a contact point — one inbox, one phone, one
address, one bank account — the sharing is a claim about control. Counting how many nominally
separate entities collapse onto each identifier turns an administrative detail into a structural
finding.

It is the cheapest signal in [[labour-fraud-analysis]] and, by the narrative's own assessment, the
strongest.

> "The prettiest evidence in the box isn't dramatic. It's a `GROUP BY`."
> — labour-fraud-analysis-a-forensic-data-investigation/docs/investigation.md, 2026-07-11

## The mechanic

One `value_counts()` over a contact column, filtered to non-empty values, sorted descending. That is
the entire computation — see [[pandas]]. In the case dataset, sixty-six workers, each with a separate
name, passport and personal file, resolve onto **two** contact inboxes: twenty-three people on the
first, twelve on the second. (No identifier or person-like value from the dataset is reproduced in
this wiki, synthetic or not.)

The interpretive move is what makes it evidence:

> "One inbox is not thirty-five people's private correspondence. One inbox is one operator holding
> thirty-five people's mail."
> — labour-fraud-analysis-a-forensic-data-investigation/docs/investigation.md, 2026-07-11

The count is not the finding. The finding is that the count contradicts the story the records tell
about themselves — independent hires who happen to share an employer.

## The graph restatement

The same relation expressed as edges gives a second reading. Build a bipartite people↔companies graph
from four document types, then count people adjacent to **two or more** companies; those bridges are
what entity succession looks like from the person's side rather than the company's. See
[[networkx]]. Degree is used only for node sizing — no centrality measure is computed, so the graph
is a picture of the same group-by, not an independent statistic.

## Why it survives anonymisation, and why that is checked

Replacing every value while preserving every relationship
([[structure-preserving-anonymisation]]) is exactly what keeps this signal readable: two source
inboxes become two fictional inboxes with the same fan-out. Because that is a property the pipeline
could silently destroy, it is asserted:

> """The 'one operator, many workers' signal must survive: an inbox shared widely."""
> — labour-fraud-analysis-a-forensic-data-investigation/src/tests/test_dataset.py, 2026-07-11

The assertion floor is deliberately far below the observed value — see [[reproducible-analysis]] for
why a loose floor is the right choice for a regenerable dataset.

## What this is not

`confidence: low` on the labelling. The README lists **entity resolution** as a demonstrated skill.
What the code performs is grouping and value-counting on an exact string. There is no blocking, no
similarity scoring, no probabilistic matching, no transitive-closure clustering — nothing that
resolves *near*-duplicates, which is what entity resolution normally means. Exact-identifier
collapse is a valid and often decisive technique; it is a different technique.

**TODO:** what was meant by "entity resolution" is unrecorded. Do not read the README's term as a

Related: the same repo's `person` table carries the contact fields the analysis treats as *shared*
across people, which sits awkwardly with its [[third-normal-form]] claim — the normalisation
"violation" and the signal are the same fact.

## Where it fits in the argument

One concentration count proves nothing on its own. It is the second of four independent weak signals
argued together as [[convergent-evidence]], each anchored to a document row through
[[chain-of-custody]].
